extracted.intended_audience: credit card issuers and stakeholders (consumer groups, trade associations, banks, credit unions), legal and regulatory commenters, and CFPB rulemaking participants
extracted.subtask_description: Evaluation and design of rules governing credit card penalty fees (late fees, returned-payment, over-the-limit, declined access check fees), including proposals for courtesy periods, dollar‑amount caps, and related disclosures and definitions. The page summarizes comments received and the CFPB's reasoning on proposed amendments to §1026.52 and related commentary.

rubrics_metrics.name: 15‑day courtesy period (proposed amendment to §1026.52(b)(2))
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether §1026.52(b)(2) should be amended to provide for a courtesy period which would prohibit late fees imposed within 15 calendar days after each payment due date.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Supporters: consumer groups, some credit unions, and others said a 15‑day courtesy period prevents abuses, helps consumers affected by mail delays, and aligns with industry practice that payments within 30 days shouldn’t be treated as late; urged applying it to safe harbor and cost‑analysis fees. Opponents: banks, credit unions, and trade associations argued it is unnecessary given 21‑day periodic statement notice, would confuse consumers about due dates and consequences (interest accrual, grace period loss, credit score impacts), weaken deterrence, raise issuers' costs and safety‑and‑soundness risks, complicate underwriting, and may exceed CFPB/TILA authority. Alternatives proposed: back‑dating fees if not paid by end of courtesy period; charge then reverse if paid within period; shorter (10‑day) period; or maintain larger safe harbor. CFPB final: declined to adopt any mandatory courtesy period absent additional evidence of net benefit, noting existing voluntary courtesy periods by some issuers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Apply courtesy period to safe harbor and cost‑analysis fees
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether a courtesy period should apply both when issuers use the safe harbor amount and when they set fees via cost analysis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consumer groups urged applying the courtesy period to both mechanisms because cost‑analysis fees are likely higher and could be triggered more frequently. CFPB considered the interactions and commenters' concerns but ultimately declined to adopt a mandatory courtesy period.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interaction with 21‑day periodic statement requirement (§1026.5(b)(2)(ii)(A))
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether the 21‑day periodic statement delivery requirement is effectively a courtesy period or conflicts with implementing a courtesy period.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Some industry commenters argued the 21‑day statement gives adequate notice and statutorily permits treating payments as late immediately, so a courtesy period would contradict that ability. CFPB responded that the 21‑day notice is not the same as a courtesy period and rejected the notion that it lacks authority to implement one, while declining to adopt the courtesy period on other grounds.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disclosures and consumer clarity about due date, interest accrual, and consequences
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether adding a courtesy period or other rule changes would allow clear disclosures so consumers understand payment due date, when interest accrues, and what consequences (late fee, loss of grace period, credit reporting impacts) follow.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Commenters warned that dual dates (minimum payment due date vs. date to avoid a late fee) would confuse consumers and make it difficult to disclose that a late fee may be avoided while other harms (interest accrual, grace-period loss) still occur. CFPB noted these concerns as part of the decision not to adopt a mandatory courtesy period.

rubrics_metrics.name: Deterrence effect and consumer payment behavior
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether a courtesy period or fee limitation would lessen deterrence and encourage late payments or otherwise alter consumer payment habits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Several industry commenters cautioned that a 15‑day courtesy period would reduce deterrence and change behavior; evidence was limited and mixed (one bank noted little evidence of habit change). CFPB weighed potential reductions in fees collected against potential consumer benefits and declined the courtesy period absent further evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Issuer costs, delinquencies, and safety‑and‑soundness impacts
rubrics_metrics.description: Assessment of how a courtesy period or fee cap would affect issuers' revenue, delinquencies, liquidity, underwriting, monitoring costs, and overall safety and soundness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Industry commenters argued the courtesy period would increase delinquencies, reduce revenue, raise costs (monitoring, collections), complicate underwriting, and potentially cause issuers to raise interest rates or other fees. CFPB acknowledged these concerns and weighed them against consumer benefits in declining to adopt the courtesy period and the proposed 25% cap.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibition on fees exceeding dollar amount associated with violation (§1026.52(b)(2)(i)(A))
rubrics_metrics.description: Section 1026.52(b)(2)(i)(A) provides that a card issuer must not impose a fee for violating account terms that exceeds the dollar amount associated with the violation; for late fees, comment 52(b)(2)(i)-1 states that the dollar amount associated with a late payment is the full amount of the required minimum periodic payment due immediately prior to assessment of the late payment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Board rationale: prohibiting fees exceeding the violation amount aligns with congressional intent to prohibit unreasonable/ disproportional penalty fees; it encourages issuers to reduce collection costs or build them into upfront rates; Board believed compliance is not overly burdensome because the required mathematical determination can be automated.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of the 'dollar amount associated with a late payment'
rubrics_metrics.description: The dollar amount associated with a late payment is the full amount of the required minimum periodic payment due immediately prior to assessment of the late payment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Industry had argued for using outstanding balance as the relevant amount; Board/CFPB explained relatively few delinquencies result in losses and the violation is failing to make the required minimum payment, not the outstanding balance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proposed 25 percent limitation on late fees
rubrics_metrics.description: CFPB proposed to amend §1026.52(b)(2)(i)(A) to limit the dollar amount associated with a late payment to 25 percent of the required minimum periodic payment due immediately prior to assessment of the late payment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rationale: make late fees more reasonable and proportional, particularly for small minimum payments; supported by data on collection contingency fees (9.5%–23%) and Y‑14 account distributions. Commenters: consumer groups generally supported the 25% restriction to prevent excessive fees on small balances; industry commenters opposed, arguing it would impede cost recovery, could raise minimum payments, and have adverse consumer and issuer consequences. CFPB ultimately decided not to adopt the 25% limitation for Larger or Smaller Card Issuers, citing issuer cost concerns and impacts on small issuers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clarification to comment 52(b)(2)(i)-1 regarding what 'minimum periodic payment' includes
rubrics_metrics.description: Proposed revision to clarify that the required minimum periodic payment due immediately prior to assessment of the late payment is the amount the consumer is required to pay to avoid the late fee, including any missed payments and fees assessed from prior billing cycles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: CFPB proposed this to avoid confusion about which payment amount the percentage limitation would apply to, given reporting practices and multiple reported payment amounts in Y‑14 responses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Application of percentage limit to other penalty fees
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether the dollar amount associated with other penalty fees covered by §1026.52(b) (over‑the‑limit, returned‑payment, declined access check fees) should be limited to 25 percent of the respective dollar amount associated with the violation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: CFPB solicited comment on examples: (1) over‑the‑limit fees limited to 25% of amount over limit; (2) returned‑payment fee limited to 25% of required minimum periodic payment prior to return; (3) declined access check limited to 25% of check amount. Consumer groups supported broader application; many industry commenters opposed extension, noting lack of analysis and potential unintended consequences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interaction of percentage cap and proposed safe harbor dollar amount
rubrics_metrics.description: How a percentage limitation (e.g., 25%) would interact with a proposed safe harbor late‑fee amount (e.g., $8) and which rule would govern when they conflict.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: CFPB analysis showed that in many cases 25% of minimum payment would be less than the proposed $8 safe harbor only for a small share of accounts (e.g., CFPB estimated ~7.7% of accounts would have been charged less than $8 under 25% limit). Commenters highlighted the possibility of fees falling below cost or altering issuer behavior; CFPB considered this in its assessment and decision not to adopt the 25% cap.

rubrics_metrics.name: System implementation and mathematical determination feasibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether issuers can program systems to perform the mathematical determinations required by dollar‑amount limitations automatically (i.e., feasibility and burden of compliance).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Board previously concluded that such mathematical determinations are generally automatable and not overly burdensome; CFPB noted this point when proposing percentage limits, though industry commenters raised concerns about upfront programming and disclosure changes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consideration of small issuers and credit unions' cost structures
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether fee limits or courtesy periods would disproportionately affect small issuers and credit unions that tend to have higher pre‑charge‑off collection costs and lower minimum payments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Commenters noted that 25% caps could dramatically reduce average late fees for some credit unions (examples: $25 -> $6.25) and that statutory limitations on some credit unions' interest rates could constrain their ability to recoup costs; CFPB acknowledged these concerns when declining the 25% proposal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Alternative fee calculation suggestions
rubrics_metrics.description: Other methods proposed for limiting or setting late/penalty fees (e.g., limit to 25% of remaining minimum after partial payment; charge 3% of total underlying debt; tie late fee to underlying balance rather than minimum payment).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consumer groups suggested 25% of remaining minimum after partial payment. An individual commenter and a bank suggested tying fee to total underlying debt (3%) or to underlying balance. Industry commenters proposed alternatives such as keeping a higher safe harbor. CFPB considered alternatives but declined to adopt these proposed changes.
